diagnosis: Symptomatic iron deficiency anaemia from menorrhagia

examinerBank.question: Walk me through your approach and differential diagnosis for this patient's anaemia.
examinerBank.modelAnswer: First confirm the anaemia is symptomatic and assess haemodynamic stability. Then classify by MCV — here it's microcytic at 68 fL with an inappropriately low reticulocyte count, suggesting impaired production rather than destruction. This narrows the differential to iron deficiency, anaemia of chronic disease, or thalassaemia. Her heavy prolonged menstrual bleeding for a year, pica, koilonychia and angular stomatitis all point to iron deficiency as the leading diagnosis, which I'd confirm with ferritin/TIBC/transferrin saturation. Anaemia of chronic disease is less likely given she is HIV negative with no TB symptoms and normal renal function, and typically shows normal or high ferritin rather than the very low ferritin expected here. Thalassaemia trait is possible with microcytosis but there's no family history and her ferritin is low rather than normal/high. I would still exclude other bleeding sources like GI loss even though menorrhagia is the obvious culprit.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Full marks for ranked, evidence-linked reasoning following the MCV/retic framework. Partial credit if student jumps straight to iron deficiency without classifying by MCV or excluding other sources.

examinerBank.question: Why is it important to ask about pica or ice-chewing in a patient you suspect has iron deficiency, and what is the proposed mechanism?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Pagophagia (ice craving) is a symptom fairly specific to iron deficiency, not seen in other anaemias. The mechanism is not fully understood but is thought to involve iron-dependent neurotransmitter or dopaminergic pathway dysfunction, and possibly a compensatory behaviour that increases cerebral blood flow or alertness in iron-deficient states. Clinically useful because it often resolves rapidly with iron repletion, even before the haemoglobin has normalised, and can be used as an early marker of treatment response.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants recognition that pica is iron-deficiency specific and ideally some attempt at the proposed mechanism, plus its use as an early marker of response to treatment.

examinerBank.question: Explain the pathophysiology behind the ejection systolic murmur you heard on cardiac examination.
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Severe anaemia reduces blood viscosity and oxygen-carrying capacity, prompting a compensatory hyperdynamic circulatory state with increased stroke volume and cardiac output. This increased flow velocity across the normal aortic and pulmonary outflow tracts creates turbulent, audible flow — a physiological or 'flow' murmur rather than structural valve disease. It typically resolves once the anaemia is corrected and the compensatory hyperdynamic state resolves.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Should distinguish this as a flow murmur secondary to hyperdynamic circulation, not structural pathology, and note it should resolve with treatment of the underlying anaemia.

examinerBank.question: Her ferritin comes back at 4 µg/L. Why is ferritin interpretation sometimes tricky in the KZN setting, and does that concern apply here?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Ferritin is an acute phase reactant, so it can be falsely elevated into the 'normal' range in the context of concurrent inflammation, infection, HIV or TB, potentially masking true iron deficiency — this is why transferrin saturation and clinical context are also used. In this patient, however, the ferritin is unambiguously very low at 4 µg/L, and she has no HIV or TB to cause a confounding inflammatory rise, so this result is a clear and reliable confirmation of true iron deficiency without needing further caveats.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Tests whether the student understands the general caveat about ferritin as an acute phase reactant in HIV/TB-endemic settings, while correctly applying critical thinking to recognise it doesn't apply in this specific case.

examinerBank.question: Why must you address the fibroids/gynaecological cause and not just replace her iron?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Oral or IV iron will correct the current haemoglobin deficit, but if the underlying cause of ongoing blood loss — fibroid-related menorrhagia — is not addressed, her monthly iron losses will continue to exceed intake and absorption, and the anaemia will recur. Definitive management requires gynaecology referral to reduce menstrual blood loss through hormonal therapy (e.g. levonorgestrel IUS, tranexamic acid) or surgical options depending on her fertility wishes, alongside correcting the anaemia itself.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants recognition that treating iron deficiency without addressing the causal bleeding source leads to recurrence — cause-directed management is essential per the framework.

framework: anaemia work-up: confirm symptomatically/haemodynamically → classify by MCV → check retic → loss vs production vs destruction → screen HIV/TB/CKD → targeted iron studies → identify bleeding source → synthesise mechanism before labelling

patient.name: Thandeka Mkhize
patient.personality: stoic, has normalised her heavy periods as 'just how I am', downplays fatigue until pressed, embarrassed discussing menstrual details
patient.openingLine: Doctor, I'm just so tired all the time now, I can hardly finish my work.

presentingComplaint: 3-month history of worsening fatigue and shortness of breath on exertion

history.fact: Fatigue has been creeping up over about 3 months, now struggles to hang washing or climb stairs at work without stopping
Gets short of breath and her heart races when she sweeps floors or carries the laundry basket, which never used to happen
Notices her heart pounding, especially when climbing stairs or carrying anything heavy
Occasional light-headedness on standing up quickly, no actual fainting
Periods have become very heavy over the past year — soaks through a pad within an hour on the heaviest days, passes large clots, bleeding lasts 8-9 days instead of her usual 5
Cycles are regular, every 26-28 days, just much heavier and longer than before
No blood in stool, no black stools, no vomiting blood, no nosebleeds, no easy bruising
Eats meat about twice a week, mostly maize meal, vegetables and beans; not vegetarian by choice, just cost
Does not drink alcohol, has never smoked
No cough, no night sweats, no fever, no weight loss — feels well otherwise apart from tiredness
Tested HIV negative 8 months ago at the clinic when she had her contraceptive injection renewed
Has been craving and chewing on ice cubes for the past two months, finds it strange but does it often
Has had heavy periods for about a year; no known fibroids diagnosed, has never had a pelvic ultrasound; last Pap smear 2 years ago was normal
No known chronic illnesses, not diabetic, not hypertensive, no previous surgery
Uses the Depo-Provera injection for contraception, takes no other regular medication, occasionally takes paracetamol for period cramps
Lives in KwaMashu with her two children and her mother; works as a domestic worker in Durban North, travels by taxi daily
No family history of thalassaemia, sickle cell disease, or bleeding disorders; mother has hypertension
No jaundice, no dark urine, no joint pains, no rash, no neurological symptoms like tingling or numbness

examination.general: Thin-built woman, conjunctival and palmar pallor marked. No jaundice, no cyanosis, no lymphadenopathy. Koilonychia noted on both index fingers. Angular stomatitis present at corners of mouth.
examination.respiratory: Chest clear, good air entry bilaterally, no crackles or wheeze
examination.cardio: Tachycardic, regular rhythm, soft ejection systolic murmur loudest at the left sternal edge, no radiation, JVP not raised, no peripheral oedema
examination.abdo: Soft, non-tender, no organomegaly, no masses palpable, bowel sounds normal
examination.neuro: Alert and orientated, no peripheral neuropathy, gait normal, reflexes normal, no ataxia

investigations.name: Full blood count
investigations.result: Hb 6.8 g/dL, MCV 68 fL (microcytic), MCH 21 pg, WCC 6.1, Platelets 468 (mildly reactive)

investigations.name: Reticulocyte count
investigations.result: Low-normal for degree of anaemia (inadequate marrow response, consistent with iron-restricted erythropoiesis)

investigations.name: Iron studies (ferritin, TIBC, transferrin saturation)
investigations.result: Ferritin 4 µg/L (low), TIBC elevated at 82 µmol/L, transferrin saturation 6% — confirms iron deficiency

investigations.name: Blood film
investigations.result: Microcytic, hypochromic red cells with anisopoikilocytosis, occasional pencil cells, no schistocytes or target cells

investigations.name: Stool for occult blood and ova/parasites
investigations.result: Negative for occult blood, no ova or parasites seen

investigations.name: Pelvic ultrasound
investigations.result: Bulky uterus with two intramural fibroids, largest 3.2 cm, no endometrial thickening, ovaries normal

investigations.name: LDH and unconjugated bilirubin
investigations.result: Both normal — no evidence of haemolysis

investigations.name: Group and crossmatch
investigations.result: O positive, 2 units held pending clinical decision on transfusion

differentials.dx: Iron deficiency anaemia secondary to menorrhagia
for: ferritin 4 µg/L with high TIBC and low transferrin saturation
history of heavy prolonged periods for a year
fibroids on ultrasound as bleeding source
normocytic or mildly microcytic picture can occur
against: ferritin is low not normal/high, arguing strongly against this pattern

for: MCV disproportionately low for degree of anaemia
against: would not respond to iron if pure trait

differentials.dx: GI source of chronic blood loss (peptic ulcer, colonic lesion)
for: iron deficiency anaemia in an adult always requires excluding a GI source
against: no PR bleeding, melaena or haematemesis
clear menstrual bleeding source already identified
age and clinical picture fit gynaecological cause

pathophys.Fatigue and exertional dyspnoea: Reduced circulating haemoglobin lowers blood oxygen-carrying capacity; tissues become relatively hypoxic, triggering compensatory tachycardia and increased cardiac output to maintain oxygen delivery, which manifests as fatigue and breathlessness on exertion
pathophys.Palpitations and tachycardia: Hyperdynamic circulation compensating for reduced oxygen-carrying capacity; reduced blood viscosity from low Hb also increases venous return and stroke volume, contributing to a hyperkinetic state
pathophys.Ejection systolic flow murmur: Increased cardiac output and reduced blood viscosity create turbulent flow across the aortic/pulmonary outflow tracts, producing an innocent flow murmur that resolves once the anaemia is corrected
pathophys.Postural drop and dizziness: Reduced circulating red cell mass and often relative intravascular volume depletion from chronic blood loss impair compensatory vasoconstriction on standing, causing symptomatic orthostatic hypotension
pathophys.Koilonychia and angular stomatitis: Iron is a cofactor for enzymes required in rapidly dividing epithelial tissue (nail matrix, oral mucosa); chronic iron deficiency impairs this turnover first in high-turnover tissues, producing spoon-shaped nails and mucosal fissuring
pathophys.Pica (ice chewing/pagophagia): Poorly understood mechanism specific to iron deficiency, postulated to involve iron-dependent neurotransmitter pathways or a compensatory oral behaviour that increases regional cerebral blood flow; resolves rapidly with iron repletion, often before Hb normalises
pathophys.Menorrhagia as the cause of iron deficie: Fibroids increase endometrial surface area and disrupt normal myometrial contraction needed for haemostasis at the spiral arterioles, leading to prolonged heavy shedding; cumulative monthly iron loss exceeds dietary iron absorption capacity, progressively depleting iron stores

staging: Severe symptomatic iron deficiency anaemia (Hb 6.8 g/dL) secondary to fibroid-related menorrhagia; haemodynamically compensated but symptomatic at rest with exertion

immediate: Assess haemodynamic stability and symptom severity; given Hb 6.8 g/dL with symptomatic tachycardia, exertional dyspnoea and postural drop, transfuse packed red cells (target symptom relief, not a fixed Hb number, per unit protocol)
Group and crossmatch already held — proceed with transfusion if symptomatic anaemia confirmed on assessment
Address active heavy bleeding: consider short-term tranexamic acid or hormonal measures to reduce menstrual blood loss while awaiting definitive gynaecological review
definitive: Oral ferrous sulfate/fumarate replacement per SA EML once haemodynamically stable, continued for at least 3-6 months after Hb normalises to replenish stores

Gynaecology referral for fibroid-related menorrhagia — options include hormonal therapy (e.g. levonorgestrel IUS, combined hormonal contraception), tranexamic acid for menstrual cycles, or surgical management (myomectomy/uterine artery embolisation) depending on fertility wishes and fibroid characteristics
IV iron if oral iron not tolerated, malabsorption suspected, or ongoing heavy losses outpace oral replacement capacity
supportive: Dietary counselling on iron-rich foods within her budget (offal, beans, dark leafy vegetables, vitamin C co-ingestion to enhance absorption)
Counsel on pica resolving with iron repletion
Explain menstrual blood loss quantification (pad/tampon counts) for monitoring response
Contraceptive counselling given ongoing Depo-Provera use and menorrhagia overlap
followUp: Repeat FBC at 2-4 weeks to confirm reticulocyte response and rising Hb trend
Repeat FBC at 3 months to confirm Hb normalisation and continue iron to replete stores
Gynaecology follow-up post-intervention to confirm reduction in menstrual blood loss
Recheck ferritin at 3-6 months once Hb normal to confirm iron store repletion before stopping supplementation

stationChecklist.item: Confirms anaemia symptomatically (fatigue, exertional dyspnoea, palpitations) and screens for haemodynamic red flags
stationChecklist.answer: Progressive fatigue, exertional dyspnoea, palpitations, postural dizziness over 3 months
stationChecklist.why: First step of the framework — confirm anaemia is symptomatic before proceeding to classification

stationChecklist.item: Takes a detailed menstrual history: flow, duration, clots, pad frequency, cycle regularity
stationChecklist.answer: Heavy bleeding soaking a pad within an hour on heavy days, large clots, 8-9 day duration, regular 26-28 day cycles, worsening over a year
stationChecklist.why: Identifies the bleeding source driving iron deficiency — core to the loss-vs-production-vs-destruction branch of the framework

stationChecklist.item: Screens for other bleeding sources (GI, urinary, epistaxis, bruising) to avoid assuming menstrual loss alone
stationChecklist.answer: No PR bleeding, melaena, haematemesis, haematuria, epistaxis or easy bruising
stationChecklist.why: Never assume a single bleeding source without excluding others, especially GI causes

stationChecklist.item: Screens for the KZN 'big four' drivers: TB symptoms, HIV status, CKD risk, dietary/nutritional history
stationChecklist.answer: No TB symptoms, HIV negative 8 months ago, no renal disease, modest meat intake twice weekly
stationChecklist.why: Mandatory background screen in any KZN anaemia work-up before attributing to a single cause

stationChecklist.item: Elicits iron-deficiency-specific symptoms such as pica/ice craving
stationChecklist.answer: Chewing ice cubes for two months
stationChecklist.why: Classic and specific symptom of iron deficiency, supports the working diagnosis before investigations return

stationChecklist.item: Performs focused examination for pallor, koilonychia, angular stomatitis/glossitis, and a cardiovascular flow murmur
stationChecklist.answer: Marked pallor, koilonychia, angular stomatitis, tachycardia with soft ejection systolic flow murmur, postural BP drop
stationChecklist.why: Confirms chronic iron deficiency signs and assesses haemodynamic compensation/decompensation

stationChecklist.item: Classifies the anaemia by MCV and reticulocyte count before generating a differential
stationChecklist.answer: Microcytic (MCV 68) with an inappropriately low reticulocyte response, indicating production failure from loss
stationChecklist.why: Central pillar of the framework — MCV and retic count direct the entire differential and investigation pathway

stationChecklist.item: Offers a ranked differential (iron deficiency anaemia vs anaemia of chronic disease vs thalassaemia vs GI blood loss) with reasoning for each
stationChecklist.why: Symptom-to-differential reasoning is the exam philosophy; must justify inclusion/exclusion of each option

stationChecklist.item: Requests FBC with film, iron studies (ferritin/TIBC/transferrin saturation), and pelvic ultrasound to confirm cause and source
stationChecklist.answer: Ferritin 4 µg/L, TIBC elevated, transferrin saturation 6%, microcytic hypochromic film, pelvic ultrasound showing fibroids
stationChecklist.why: Confirmatory pathway for iron deficiency plus identification of the bleeding source per the framework

stationChecklist.item: Recognises Hb 6.8 g/dL with symptomatic/haemodynamic compromise as a transfusion indication and initiates group & crossmatch
stationChecklist.answer: Symptomatic anaemia at Hb 6.8 g/dL with tachycardia and postural drop warrants packed red cell transfusion per unit protocol
stationChecklist.why: Red flag recognition — symptomatic severe anaemia requires urgent transfusion work-up, not just oral iron

stationChecklist.item: Outlines definitive cause-directed management: oral/IV iron replacement, gynaecology referral for fibroid-related menorrhagia, and duration of iron therapy
stationChecklist.answer: Oral ferrous sulfate for 3-6 months post Hb normalisation, gynaecology referral for hormonal or surgical management of fibroids, IV iron if oral not tolerated
stationChecklist.why: Treating the anaemia without addressing the ongoing menstrual blood loss source will lead to recurrence
